name: Adam Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weekdays from three until eight I teach drums in the soundproofed back room of a music shop on Station Street, mostly kids and a few dads having a midlife moment. Friday and Saturday nights I play in a function band: weddings, birthdays, office parties, the full cheesy set. I load the kit into a borrowed van, play four hours, and get home at two.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good is a dance floor going off when we hit the first chorus of a song everyone knows. Hard is the money, because the shop pays me eighteen a lesson and the band pays a hundred and ten a night, and neither is guaranteed. I live with my girlfriend Sofia, who works early shifts at a bakery, so we pass each other at the door most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: people will always want a band at a wedding. I'd probably joke about it on the band's page. Nobody I know cares much about AI talk anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, AI was never my biggest worry. The shop owner, Dev, told me in October that sales are down a fifth and he might close the teaching room to save on heating. My real worry isn't a robot drummer, it's a music shop owner turning the heating off in my teaching room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to teach some pupils from home on a practice kit with mesh heads, so the neighbours don't kill me, in case the shop closes the room. I'd chase the band's agent for more midweek bookings. And I'd use the AI chat thing now and then for invoices and the band's emails, like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tense. It's not a disaster, but I've got about three weeks of money and a lot of maybes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the shop did close the teaching room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lose about sixty percent of my income overnight. I'd move the pupils I could to my place, maybe half of them, and look for something on weekdays, warehouse work or deliveries. I've done delivery driving before and hated it, but it pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Sofia say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sofia's practical, more than me. She says pick a date, and if the shop's no better by then, get a weekday job and keep drumming at weekends. She's probably right, but I keep moving the date.

say: People will always want a **live band** at a wedding.
I'd make a **joke** about it on the band's page and move on.
think: AI was never my **biggest worry**; the shop's finances are.
Sales are down **a fifth**, and the teaching room might close.
do: Set up a **mesh-head kit** at home to teach some pupils.
Chase the band's **agent** for midweek bookings.
Keep using an **AI chat tool** now and then for invoices and emails.
feel: A bit **tense**, with **three weeks** of money and a lot of maybes.
S0.quote: My real worry isn't a robot drummer, it's a music shop owner turning the heating off in my teaching room.
fieldNote: His biggest threat is a **struggling shop**, not AI, even in AI Plateau.
Losing the teaching room would cut about **sixty percent** of his income.
His girlfriend Sofia wants a **deadline**, and he keeps moving it.

steps.text: Set up a mesh-head practice kit at home for some pupils
Chase the band's agent for midweek bookings
Use an AI chat tool for band invoices and emails

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say drummers are fine, we hit things for a living and computers can't do that. Then I'd admit the band's admin and bookings are going to change, because the agent already uses software. I'd probably say it's a good time to be a live musician, which might be half true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the playing is safe for now but the money around it isn't. Couples might pick a cheaper band booked through an app, and parents might buy a learn-drums app with a mat for their kid. Nobody's going to replace me behind a drum kit soon, but they can replace the shop that pays me and the agent that books me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start booking the band directly myself, with a website and the AI tools that answer enquiries, once I'd seen another band make it work. I'd build up home teaching so I'm not relying on Dev's shop. I'd keep an eye on warehouse jobs, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. It's a slow squeeze, and I can see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the AI tools once you'd seen another band do it. Which band?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a band from the next town, the Velvet Hours, who've cut their agent out and fill their diary themselves. Their singer told me the software answers enquiries at midnight. If they're still busy in six months, I'd copy them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the band would struggle most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our singer, Marta, who also does the band's bookings and paperwork. If software does that, her extra cut goes. She's got a little boy, so I'd worry about her more than me.

The band's **admin and bookings** are going to change, though.

Keep an eye on **warehouse jobs** just in case.
feel: **Anxious** but **not frozen**, watching a slow squeeze.

fieldNote: He sees his **hands-on** playing as safe but the **business around it** as exposed.

steps.text: Build a band website with an AI tool that answers enquiries

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we all need to stick together and look after each other, and the government needs a proper plan, fast. I'd be careful online, because people get nasty about this stuff. At gigs I'd keep playing and keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and all the thinking work goes, including the ordering at Sofia's bakery and my agent's whole job. The drumming is hands-on, so I'd get until 2031, but the people paying for weddings might not have jobs. If the couples who book us lose their office jobs in 2028, nobody's paying a function band in 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a steady weekday job straight away, probably at the distribution warehouse by the bypass, because it's hands-on and hiring. I'd keep the band at weekends while there's work, and I'd sell the car to cut the insurance. Sofia and I would look at moving in with her parents to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like being in a band where the tempo suddenly doubles and nobody told you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The warehouse is hands-on, but robots come about three years later. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, warehouses are probably first for robots. But three years of wages while I work out the next thing is better than three years of hoping. I'd probably look at something like fitting or repair work after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving in with Sofia's parents. How would that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Her dad would let me practise in the garage and then complain about it every day. It'd be fine for a year. Longer than that and I'd want my own front door back.

say: We need to **stick together**, and the government needs a plan, fast.
I'd keep playing at gigs and **keep quiet** online.
think: All the **thinking work** goes in two years, including my agent's job.
Couples who lose **office jobs** in 2028 won't book a band in 2029.
do: Take a **warehouse job** by the bypass straight away.
**Sell the car** to cut insurance and running costs.
Move in with Sofia's **parents** to save rent.
feel: **Alarmed**, like a song where the **tempo** suddenly doubles.

fieldNote: He sees his customers' **office jobs** as the weak point, not his drumming.
He knows warehouses face **robots** early but values three years of wages.
Moving in with Sofia's parents works for **a year**, not longer.

steps.text: Take a weekday job at the warehouse by the bypass
Sell the car to save on insurance and running costs
Move in with Sofia's parents for about a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people stop arguing and plan. I'd tell younger drummers to learn a trade alongside the sticks. Online I'd keep it practical, not political.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years means the band work keeps going for a while, and the drumming lasts until about 2034. The teaching shrinks as apps get better, and the shop probably goes. With five years' warning, I'd stop pretending a drummer doesn't need a second trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time course in instrument repair, or maybe general electrical work, in the evenings at the college, about six hundred a year. I'd keep teaching and gigging. I'd use AI for the boring admin by then, because everyone would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have something to do with it. Doing something helps me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why instrument repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've fixed half the shop's drum kits for free already, so I know I like it. Drums break, and people will want a person to look at them for a while yet. I'm guessing, but it feels sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything change between you and Sofia in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop putting off talking about a deposit for a flat, because the longer we wait the worse it gets. We'd probably start saving fifty each a month, even if it's slow. Sofia would like a date for everything, and she'd get one.

say: Five years is **enough to get ready** if people stop arguing.
Younger drummers should learn a **trade** alongside the sticks.
think: The band and the **drumming** last until about 2034.
Teaching shrinks as **apps** improve, and the shop probably goes.
do: Study **instrument repair** in the evenings for about six hundred a year.
Save **fifty each** a month with Sofia for a flat deposit.
feel: **Anxious**, but doing something with the worry helps.
S3.quote: With five years' warning, I'd stop pretending a drummer doesn't need a second trade.
fieldNote: He picks **repair work** because he already fixes the shop's kits for free.
The warning pushes him to plan a **flat deposit** with Sofia at last.
He's **pragmatic**: he'd use AI for admin because everyone would be.

steps.text: Take an evening instrument repair course at the college
Keep teaching drums and playing weekend gigs
Save fifty a month each with Sofia for a flat deposit
Use AI tools for the band's bookings and admin

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so let's do it properly: apprenticeships, retraining, and help for people who get caught out. I'd tell my pupils to keep playing, because you can't download what it feels like to play with other people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'd be thirty-seven, and the drumming lasts till about 2039. I'd probably drift for the first few years, if I'm honest. Ten years is long enough for me to waste five of them, and my girlfriend Sofia would remind me of every single one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same idea as the five-year one, just less rushed. A repair course over two years, then try to rent a small unit for repairs and lessons together, maybe with Dev from the shop if he's still going. And keep the band as long as people are getting married.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. Still that money knot, because none of this fixes next month's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd drift for a few years. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sofia, mostly, and a deadline written down. If I've not signed up for the course by next September, she's allowed to sign me up herself. We've actually agreed things like that before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change anything bigger at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably get engaged. We've talked about it, and the band plays enough weddings that I know what they cost. With ten years I'd feel I could plan one, small.

say: Ten years is plenty for **apprenticeships**, retraining and help for people caught out.
Pupils should keep playing, because you can't **download** playing with others.

I could easily **waste five years** of the ten drifting.
do: Do the **repair course** over two years.
Rent a small **repair-and-lessons unit**, maybe with Dev from the shop.
Keep the **band** going while people still marry.
feel: **Okay**, mostly, with a **money knot** about next month's rent.

steps.text: Sign up for the instrument repair course by next September

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the people who book bands lose their jobs before the robots even come for mine. What would help is proper retraining money and some help with rent while you switch, so you're not choosing between a course and eating.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the body. Drumming for four hours at a wedding leaves my wrists aching, and I'd still rather do that than sit at a screen.

headlineQuote: Drumming for four hours at a wedding leaves my wrists aching, and I'd still rather do that than sit at a screen.
portrait: Adam is a **27-year-old drummer** who teaches at a music shop and plays weekend weddings.
He lives with his girlfriend Sofia, a bakery worker, on about **three weeks** of savings.
He's **pragmatic**, uses AI now and then, and copies what works for other bands.
He sees his **hands-on** drumming as safe, but the shop and his customers as exposed.
Given time, he'd add **instrument repair** as a second trade, if Sofia holds him to a deadline.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because couples lose their jobs before robots reach drumming.
whatWouldHelp: **Retraining money**, plus help with **rent** during the switch.
